paras: The lynching of Morgan Hamilton was the shooting of a Black farm worker by a party of men carrying an arrest warrant in a field near Booneville, Mississippi, on the morning of Saturday, June 17, 1882. Hamilton had been accused of the murder of Miss Serena Benton and released by the inquest jury; the eight or ten men who went to re-arrest him shot him as he ran, and the sheriff set out after them. A Mississippi correspondent called the killing an outrage committed "on mere suspicion," while wire copy carried it across the country as the shooting of an accused murderer.

Serena J. Benton, an unmarried former school teacher of about sixty who owned a farm, was beaten to death beside the road five miles west of Booneville in late May, and her body was found days later by a Black man, L. Simmons. While the inquest was still sitting, Morgan Hamilton was in jail "as being implicated in the murder." A Jackson dispatch added that one of her rings had been found in his possession, a detail the Mississippi accounts do not repeat.

According to the Vicksburg Herald's correspondent, the inquest jury found only a little circumstantial evidence and discharged Hamilton. The Booneville Pleader likewise wrote that he had been rigidly examined and released, and said it did not know what new evidence justified his re-arrest. Some residents then swore out an affidavit before G. C. Walters, a justice of the peace, who issued a warrant for Hamilton's arrest.

On Saturday morning a party went to the field where Hamilton was at work to serve the warrant; the Vicksburg correspondent and the wire counted eight men, the Pleader ten. In the correspondent's version the men, "without any excuse," told him to run and shot him dead as he started off. The Pleader's account was that the party arrested him without trouble and that he broke away on the road to the justice, though it noted a report that some of the men had told him to run.

By the Pleader's count he was struck by thirty-four bullets from two shotguns and a pistol at fifteen or twenty paces. He ran about 150 yards with one man chasing him on foot, then fell and died within minutes.

The sheriff went to the scene the same day to arrest the party, but its members had fled. As of the Pleader's issue of June 22 no arrests had been made, and no later report of arrests, an inquest on Hamilton or a trial appears in the coverage. The Vicksburg correspondent wrote that the county's "good citizens" were not in sympathy with the killing and hoped all concerned would be brought to justice.

The fullest reports came from Mississippi correspondents, and both distanced themselves from the killers. The Memphis Public Ledger ran the Vicksburg Herald's special under the headline "An Outrage in Mississippi. A Colored Man Foully Assassinated on Mere Suspicion of a Crime." The Booneville Pleader, reprinted in the Ripley Advertiser on July 1, set out "the facts" and left readers to form their own conclusions, while calling such violations of the law regrettable and punishable.

The New Orleans Times-Democrat's special reached the Savannah Morning News and the St. Paul Daily Globe on June 19 and the Waco Daily Examiner on June 20. Its headlines, "An Accused Murderer Riddled" and "Murdering an Alleged Murderer," put the accusation first, though the text called the killers "the murderers." Shortened versions ran in the Salt Lake Herald, the Middlebury Register, the Raleigh Farmer and Mechanic and the Bolivar Bulletin, and as a single line in crime columns of the Watertown Republican and the Mower County Transcript.
In late June the Hand County Press and the Crawford Avalanche used a different brief, saying Hamilton "was lynched at Booneville, Miss., on suspicion," and paired it with a Tennessee lynching.

Accounts differ on the size of the party, eight in the wire and the Vicksburg report and ten in the Pleader, and on whether Hamilton was shot when first approached or after his arrest. Relayed wire copy said "yesterday" from later datelines, but the Booneville-datelined reports and the Pleader place the killing on Saturday, June 17.

bases: A party of eight to ten private men holding a justice's warrant shot Hamilton, accused of murder and earlier released by an inquest jury, after telling him to run; the sheriff then sought them (A8, A16, A4).

Eight (A4, A8) or ten (A16) men killed Hamilton, accused of the Benton murder, under color of an arrest warrant; the sheriff went to arrest them and the local paper called it a violation of the law (A8, A16), and a later brief called it a lynching (A13).

The Vicksburg Herald correspondent (A8), the Times-Democrat wire (A4, A5) and the Booneville Pleader (A16) independently report the killing by a warrant party in or near the field; they differ on size and details.

accounts.label: Vicksburg Herald correspondent
accounts.gist: Hamilton had been discharged by the inquest jury; people swore out a fresh affidavit, and the eight men sent to serve the warrant 'without any excuse' told him to run and shot him; local citizens disapproved.

accounts.label: Booneville Pleader (local)
accounts.gist: Ten men arrested him easily in the field; on the way to the justice he ran and was riddled with thirty-four bullets, running 150 yards before he fell; it was 'even reported' he had been told to run; the party fled and no arrests were made.

Wire versions ran under 'An Accused Murderer Riddled' and 'Murdering an Alleged Murderer', describing the victim as an accused murderer and the killers as murderers.
Midwestern weeklies reduced it to one line in crime columns, two saying Hamilton was 'lynched ... on suspicion'.
